cards.title: AI and carbon emissions
cards.script:
https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/ai-and-climate-change#abstract

The increased energy efficiency from AI would more than offset the new carbon emissions. It is estimated carbon emissions could increase by nearly 500 MtCO2 with the very high adoption. The IEA estimates, from optimization alone, it could save 1400 MtCO2! In other words, investing in AI will yield climate returns.

"The adoption of existing AI applications in end-use sectors could lead to 1 400 Mt of CO2 emissions reductions in 2035 in the Widespread Adoption Case. This does not include any breakthrough discoveries that may emerge thanks to AI in the next decade. These potential emissions reductions, if realised, would be three times larger than the total data centre emissions in the Lift-off Case, and four times larger than those in the Base Case"

Energy use. Somewhere around 0.3 Wh per prompt.  Hannah Ritchie summarizes a few here.

[https://hannahritchie.substack.com/p/ai-footprint-august-2025?utm_campaign=posts-open-in-app&triedRedirect=true](https://hannahritchie.substack.com/p/ai-footprint-august-2025?utm_campaign=posts-open-in-app&triedRedirect=true)

cards.title: AI water use
cards.script:
Andy Masley [uses](https://open.substack.com/pub/andymasley/p/a-cheat-sheet-for-conversations-about?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=1rrrnf) Google's report that an average prompt uses about 2 mL of water. That's mostly from the power generator. The data center itself uses 0.3mL per prompt.

The median American has more than a [400 gallon per day](https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/22/3007/2018/) water foot print.

UC Riverside [study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.03271) estimates 16.9 mL per prompt.

cards.title: Fixing the budget in the back of the poor
cards.subtitle: The quest to shrink "the deserving poor"
cards.script:
Is it true that the government spends $181,000 per family in poverty? And because poverty persists, does that imply the whole system is bungled up in waste?

No.

A new op ed from the editorial board of the [Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/interactive/2026/09/14/safety-net-spending-has-surged-wheres-money-going/) attempts to frame our recent federal budget issues around an excess of generosity.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789423686792-q64m.jpg){md}

To get that number, they calculate the total spending on Medicaid, Food Stamps, Housing, Pell Grants, and other programs, which is $1.3T and then divided that by those that live below the official poverty line - or around 10% of the population (340M*0.1=34M)

$1.26T/34M = $37k per person.

But the trick here is the denominator. No - the average person in poverty doesn't receive $37k in assistance. Other people do too!

Two things are going on here. First, this is a sloppy attempt at solving our budget issues by simply addressing "fraud." For evidence the op-ed cites a partisan think tank's calculation of 6 million people signing up for ACA premium subsidies.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789423721604-bvs2.png){md}

Yet, this number is not accepted outside of partisan circles. It is disputed on ground of bad methodology, including [double counting](https://kffhealthnews.org/health-care-costs/aca-marketplace-subsidies-tax-credits-insurance-federal-government-shutdown-fraud/). The [Government Accountability Office](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108742) estimated a number closer to 160,000 for 2024. Please understand, this is an important problem that needs fixing, but it is a number 97% smaller than the one cited in the op-ed.

The second thing - what really frames the argument - is narrowing who qualifies as what is often called "the deserving poor." Those who are poor enough; destitute enough; disadvantaged enough to merit either your personal private charity or the social safety net of the government.

Take this graph, complaining that the growth in Medicaid. Particularly after the growth in Obamacare is now 26% of the population. The official poverty rate is 10%.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789423694578-jl9k.jpg)

Does poverty end once you cross that magic threshold? That is, today for a family of four $33,000. Would you be fine if you made $40k? Of course not. In fact when we ask folks, 73% of the population say they're doing okay or living comfortably financially. That leaves 27% of folks struggling.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789423698041-j9pz.png)

I've long said on this channel that the median American is doing fine (excluding recent Iran war caused gas price pain). But the bottom quarter are having difficulties. This same source shows 16% of adults did not pay all their bills in full last month. 26% of the population skipped medical treatment because of cost.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789423696300-p25j.jpg)

Giving the game away, after complaining that 12% of the population is too high to be on food stamps, they give an Orwellian turn of phrase somehow claiming that it is false to brand recent Medicaid reforms as "cuts"  when its actually just gradually nudging spending back to before. A cut is a cut.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789423692538-qq7e.jpg){md}

Now, I'm in favor of finding ways to increase efficiency, but when it comes to balancing our federal budget, I find it wickedly immoral by enlightened utilitarian principles, Christian ethics, or any other major moral system to place that burden on the backs of the more vulnerable among us.

When nearly half of social security payments go to the upper middle class or wealthy, why are we claiming some family making $40k a year is somehow too prosperous to need assistance. Please.

![](data/images/c17qt2fb-1789596624071-cev7.png)

cards.title: Economic Explained and Liars
cards.script:
I have a very low tolerance for liars.

Today, I'm going to discuss one such prominent liar in the Economic Communication space.

The most popular econ channel on YouTube is Economics Explains.

His most recent video claims "Economics is a Junk Science."

![[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TsfsoaNFyTQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TsfsoaNFyTQ)](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788807506172-l06y.jpg)

Now, good science depends on criticism and, when rigorously done, is welcome.

Yet, this isn't good criticism. Instead it's peddling a certain sensationalist doomerism. Oh - and he's a liar - which I'll prove at the end of the video.

He opens the video by claiming without citation "Economists have famously predicted 15 out of the last 2 recessions."

But, as my own channel has consistently said during Democratic and Republican presidents - no, [we aren't seeing a recession](https://www.tiktok.com/@econchrisclarke/video/7326606692852976939)

https://www.tiktok.com/@econchrisclarke/video/7326606692852976939

Do you know who has repeatedly made videos about the oncoming catastrophe? Economics Explained. Claiming Stagflation 11 months ago; a year ago saying This is the Recession the US Needs to Have; the Rise and Fall of the USA; to even predicting we're ahead of schedule for the collapse of society by 2040.

![It's rather rich for a video claiming "Economics is a Junk Science" because it falsely predicts recessions that never happens, when the own channel is built upon selling economic doom to its viewers.](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788808551482-d7mg.png)

I started following the channel when it was very young before Covid. But when the economy started seeing an uptick in inflation, I noticed a turn towards sensationalism.

An April 2021 video claimed "Hyperinflation is Already Here" with comparisons to Weimar Republic Germany 1922. 3 million views.

![](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788808907810-2zra.jpg)

The problem is its not true.

While we saw more inflation than we're used to, topping out at annual 9% in June 2022, this is not hyperinflation.

![[https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=1Ygm3](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=1Ygm3)](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788809001210-3bwf.png)

There are around 50 documented incidences of hyperinflation in history. Germany 1922 comes in as the 5th highest with a **MONTHLY **inflation rate of *29,500%*!

![[https://object.cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/pubs/pdf/hanke-krus-hyperinflation-table-may-2013.pdf](https://object.cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/pubs/pdf/hanke-krus-hyperinflation-table-may-2013.pdf)](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788809227102-z7gz.png)

Since this is measured in monthly, let's convert the U.S. recent experience from the customary twelve-month to the monthly rate. At our peak it was 1.2% per month!

![This is the month over month inflation rate.](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788809503389-hh8n.png)

For more critics of the sloppiness of these video essays, see the great channel, [Money and Macro](https://www.youtube.com/@MoneyMacro) by Dr. Joeri Schasfoort. Here are two videos, in particular, where he meticulously combats Economics Explained's falsehoods.

![[https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGbVoSdwvesDzFMtPSBVOgDn5RejWf1dN](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGbVoSdwvesDzFMtPSBVOgDn5RejWf1dN)](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788810076190-7nbm.png)

Now, let's come to the lie. In their pitch to sponsors, such as the one on Passion Froot dot me - an AI marketing tool - the host self describes as "esteemed economics professor Michael Burnand." Here's another [source](https://jobs.thepublishpress.com/company/economics-explained).

![[https://www.passionfroot.me/economics-explained](https://www.passionfroot.me/economics-explained)](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788813633468-zwi6.png)

So, who is Michael Burnand? I found his LinkedIn page.

![](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788807205764-ua2w.png)

Showing undergrad and master's degrees in Economics. It appears he started his channel while he was attending his Master's on the side.

![](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788804212976-b2bt.jpg)

Now, I want to be very clear: you don't need to have a PhD to be an economist and do high quality work - especially in econ-journalism. Kyla Scanlon, WSJ's Greg Ip, Joey Politano all do fantastic work.

But...they also don't present themselves as "esteemed economics professors."

So, what is his professional experience? After the success of his YouTube channel, he [sold ](https://www.airwavemedia.com/post/airwave-signs-deal-with-economics-explained)it to Lunar X and now works at Providence Finance doing personal finance advising.

![](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788807187996-yc9u.png)

![](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788804216670-5ifm.jpg)

Look, I'll repeat. I welcome everybody's comments and perspectives. Everyone operates in the economy, and everyone has opinions on it.

But, here's my last question. Just like Oren Cass - the tariff loving partisan lawyer who gave himself the title "Chief Economist" at his own think tank. If Economics truly is a "Junk Science" then why do these guys flout fake econ titles?

![](data/images/ccrl0hcj-1788807021583-7520.png)
cards.subtitle: Sensationalism breeds virality, harming truth, fostering liars.

cards.title: Venezuela American Oil Deal
cards.script:
![[https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp](https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp)](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013451578-ei0v.jpg)

Will the US take over of Venezuelan oil fields lower gas prices? Let's take a look.

![](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013236533-38vp.jpg)

Historically, Venezuela produced around 2.5 mbd. But since the crash in oil prices are the end of 2014 and the gross mismanagement of the Maduro administration, production has fallen to around 1 mbd. - so we are looking at an increase of 1-2 mbd.

![[https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/images/Fig2.png](https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/images/Fig2.png)](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013238685-pa34.jpg)

Now let's compare to global output. Before the war, the globe produced around 105 mbd, the latest data shows that fell to 95 - a gap of ten.

I don't think we need any fancy math to know that two is smaller than ten.

But there are other issues.

1. It will take years of capital investment to get production back up to historical levels.

The second is a lot more interesting. Trump appears to be our most socialist president ever. This new supposed deal in Venezuela places the U.S. government as a majority shareholder.

![[https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp](https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp)](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013942776-49d1.jpg)

While defining capitalism and socialism can involve a lot of variables, my simple one sentence version is, "Who owns the means of production?"

We're seeing a broader trend by the current administration. A move towards more state ownership of the means of production. The government now has stakes in [30 different firms](https://www.cato.org/blog/government-ownership-stakes-companies-becoming-routine-under-trump).

The arguments in favor - an argument repeated by socialists, such as Bernie Sanders, note that the Federal Government often gives favorable tax breaks or grants to businesses without any return back to the government. That is beyond the general macroeconomic improvements these policies are designed for. Instead, if the government owns stocks, it would then share in some of the profits.

Well, why haven't we been doing this all along? We can point to 150 years years of attempts to make these arrangements work.

As Giacomo Corneo points out in his excellent book, "Is Capitalism Obsolete? A Journey Through Alternative Economic Systems"

"Sometimes state involvement has worked, and sometimes it has not. Typically it has not when governments imposed business decisions on management and misused enterprises under their control for party-political ends."

Government ownership changes the incentive structure. Rather than consumers and other business competitors disciplining a firm to operate efficiently, firms specialize in pleasing government leaders to receive profits.

The consumers end up worse. Inefficient and cost burdened firms are propped up longer than they should. We get waste instead of winning.

cards.title: Did Capitalism Drain The Colorado?
cards.script:
Is capitalism to blame for the overuse of the Colorado River?

Afterall, profits mean water extraction.

Golf courses in the desert. High rise condos. Sprawling Metropolises.

[https://www.tiktok.com/@econchrisclarke/video/7681098050533690655](https://www.tiktok.com/@econchrisclarke/video/7681098050533690655)

However, there's just one problem with this narrative - The Colorado River is not run by the unadulterated free market.

It's central planning with feudal characteristics.

Here's what I mean.

1. There's no real functioning water market.  Yes, there's some markets for temporary leasing inside a state. But you can't plan big long-term projects like that.

The government decided 150 years ago how much water a particular plot of land can extract. And those - now practically ancient - water claims keep getting past down from generation to generation like the feudal lords of old.

2. Unlike other assets in capitalism, it's use it or lose it. No incentive for thriftiness or storing for the future.

Result: the classic soviet-style waste you get from central planning.

But wait, it sounds like we're talking about large tracts of land and farming. Aren't the big cities and the 40 million people relying on the Colorado River the real ones to blame?

No. Here is the sources and uses of the Colorado River.

![[Richter et al (2024) New Water Account Reveals Why Water No Longer Reaches The Sea](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-024-01291-0)](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787843787982-roqu.png)

Most the water enters in the Upper Basin largely through snowmelt from the Rockies.

Now, look at MCI: Municipal, Commercial, and Industrial use. It's a very small share compared to agriculture. And that agriculture is largely devoted to growing alfalfa and hay, an incredibly low-value cash crop.

![[Richter et al (2025) Reducing Irrigation of Livestock Feed is Essential to Saving Great Salt Lake](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312)](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787850314567-m1k6.png)

It's not just the Colorado. The Great Salt Lake Basin shows a similar pattern.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1788374785590-g3u7.jpg)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1788382858129-4o6k.png)

The Salt Lake is declining every decade. Lakes Powell and Mead are now near record lows.

It's [estimated](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312) that we need to reduce water use by more than 25% just to stabilize the reservoirs.

So, where should the cuts happen?

If you ask an economist - we'd say the lowest value activity.

And...markets are a pretty great way to reveal that information.

We've already done this. It's how we solved the Acid Rain problem back in the 90's.

We need a "cap and trade" for the Colorado and Great Salt Lake.

Today, farmers profits are boosted on the backs of working families. Farmers pay on avg $30 per acre foot compared to the $512 dollars the rest of us pay.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787839527433-2ecs.jpg)

![[https://cawaterlibrary.net/document/free-water-while-it-lasts-an-analysis-of-wholesale-water-pricing-in-the-lower-colorado-river-basin-states/](https://cawaterlibrary.net/document/free-water-while-it-lasts-an-analysis-of-wholesale-water-pricing-in-the-lower-colorado-river-basin-states/)](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787839529928-4pt1.jpg)

We call this rent seeking. Earning profits not because you produce what society values most, but because you force society to give you more than what you produce. If you can't pay the real costs - you shouldn't be producing it.

In The Great Salt Lake Basin, hay and alfalfa only contribute 0.07% to the economy.

![[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312)](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1788385475061-bwa9.png)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849131550-qpuw.jpg)

What if we just paid the farmers off? It would be less than an annual Netflix subscription per person. But I gotta be honest, it's sits uneasy that in perpetuity, farmers and their descendants get free cash from the public, just cuz of some great great grandad.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849133071-jrkt.jpg)

The debate is about cultural issues, not economics or food security. It's the lifestyles of the 20k farmers and ranchers in the basin. That is, in a region of 2.8M, why are we giving out cultural sympathy points to businesses that produce a low value product?

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849134938-vvr4.jpg)

That ain't capitalism.

We need more well regulated water markets, not historical feudal water claims. The Salt Lake and Colorado River Basins can support cities two or even three times as large, doubling the economy. All while preserving even more water for environmental needs.
cards.subtitle: Or was it Central Planning with Fuedal Characteristics?
